title: Ratios and Business Metrics
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of ratios and business metrics.
Apply conversion rates in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.

content.intro: Learn ratios and business metrics through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Ratios and Business Metrics matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: In ratios and business metrics, define the unit of analysis before writing the query: one row per customer, order, day, or other grain. Make filters, NULL handling, time boundaries, and tie-breaking rules visible in the SQL.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Conversion rates, Average order value, Ratios and percentage calculations, Rates with zero denominators. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Conversion rates
items.text: Conversion rates works best when inputs and outputs have deliberate types. Use explicit casts when intent is unclear, guard against overflow or truncation, and avoid converting typed values to display strings before calculations finish.

items.title: Average order value
items.text: Average order value helps you use SQL for reporting and analysis with the right grain, time buckets, windows, distribution statistics, and business metric definitions. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Ratios and percentage calculations
items.text: Ratios and percentage calculations begins with a definition of the metric and its grain. Name the numerator, denominator, time zone, null policy, and tie-handling rule before translating the definition into SQL.

items.text: Rates with zero denominators summarizes rows. Decide the grain of the result first, group only by the dimensions that define one output row, and verify NULL and duplicate behavior in each metric.

content_blocks.code: SELECT SUM(total_amount) FILTER (WHERE status = 'completed') / NULLIF(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'completed'), 0) AS avg_completed_order FROM orders;
content_blocks.expected_output: NULLIF prevents division by zero. Define the population and the currency/precision rules before presenting a business metric.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

hints: Begin with the subtopic conversion rates and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
